title: Aqueduct (water supply)
wiki_lead:
An aqueduct is a watercourse constructed to carry water from a source to a distribution point far away. In modern engineering, the term aqueduct is used for any system of pipes, ditches, canals, tunnels, and other structures used for this purpose. The term aqueduct also often refers specifically to a bridge carrying an artificial watercourse. 
Aqueducts were used in ancient Greece, the ancient Near East, ancient Rome (name gained from Latin: aquaeductus) and pre-Columbian Mexico and Peru. The simplest aqueducts are small ditches cut into the earth. Much larger channels may be used in modern aqueducts. Aqueducts sometimes run for some or all of their path through tunnels constructed underground. Modern aqueducts may also use pipelines. Historically, agricultural societies have constructed aqueducts to irrigate crops and supply large cities with drinking water.

The term aqueduct also often refers specifically to a bridge carrying an artificial watercourse. 
Aqueducts were used in ancient Greece, the ancient Near East, ancient Rome (name gained from Latin: aquaeductus) and pre-Columbian Mexico and Peru. The simplest aqueducts are small ditches cut into the earth. Much larger channels may be used in modern aqueducts. Aqueducts sometimes run for some or all of their path through tunnels constructed underground. Modern aqueducts may also use pipelines. Historically, agricultural societies have constructed aqueducts to irrigate crops and supply large cities with drinking water.


Etymology
The word aqueduct is derived from the Latin words aqua (water) and ductus (led or guided).


Ancient aqueducts

Although particularly associated with the Romans, aqueducts were devised much earlier in Greece, the Near East, Nile Valley, and Indian subcontinent, where people such as the Egyptians and Harappans built sophisticated irrigation systems. The Aztecs and Incans also built such systems independently later. Roman-style aqueducts were used as early as the 7th century BC, when the Assyrians built an 80 km long limestone aqueduct, which included a 10 m high section to cross a 300 m wide valley, to carry water to their capital city, Nineveh.


Crete
Although particularly associated with the Romans, aqueducts were likely first used by the Minoans around 2000 BC. The Minoans had developed what was then an extremely advanced irrigation system, including several aqueducts.


Deccan

The Indian subcontinent is believed to have some of the earliest aqueducts. Evidence can be found at the sites of present-day Hampi, Karnataka. The massive aqueducts near Tungabhadra River supplying irrigation water were once 15 miles (24 km) long. The waterways supplied water to royal bath tubs.


Oman

In Oman from the Iron Age, in Salut, Bat, and other sites, a system of underground aqueducts called falaj or qanāts were constructed, a series of well-like vertical shafts, connected by gently sloping horizontal tunnels.
There are three types of falaj:

Daudi (داوودية) with underground aqueducts
Ghaili (الغيلية ) requiring a dam to collect the water
Aini (العينية ) whose source is a water spring
These enabled large scale agriculture to flourish in a dry land environment.


Persia

In Persia, starting around 3000 years ago  a system of underground aqueducts called qanāts were constructed, a series of well-like vertical shafts, connected by gently sloping tunnels. This technique:

taps into subterranean water in a manner that delivers water to the surface without the need for pumping. The water drains relied on gravity, with the destination lower than the source, which is typically an upland aquifer.
allows water to be transported long distances in hot dry climates without losing a large proportion of the source water to seepage and evaporation.


Levant

Throughout Petra, Jordan, the Nabataean engineers took advantage of every natural spring and every winter downpour to channel water where it was needed. They constructed aqueducts and piping systems that allowed water to flow across mountains, through gorges and into the temples, homes, and gardens of Petra's citizens. Walking through the Siq, one can easily spot the remains of channels that directed water to the city center, as well as durable retention dams that kept powerful flood waters at bay.
In ancient Judea and neighboring territories (in today's Israel and the West Bank), aqueducts evolved from simple channels dug into the earth, as seen at Khirbet Qumran, into more advanced systems of hewn or built stone sealed with waterproof plaster and covered with stone slabs to prevent contamination. Beginning in the Hellenistic period
grok_lead: An aqueduct is an engineered conduit or system designed to transport water from a source to a destination, typically over long distances and often relying on gravity to facilitate flow through open channels, closed pipes, tunnels, bridges, and supporting structures. These systems have been essential for supplying fresh water for drinking, irrigation, sanitation, and industrial uses in urban and agricultural settings since ancient times. Aqueducts represent remarkable feats of civil engineering, balancing hydraulic principles like flow velocity and pressure with structural integrity using materials such as stone, masonry, and later concrete or steel. The development of aqueducts traces back to prehistoric and early civilizations, with initial innovations appearing in Minoan Crete around 3000 BC, where terracotta pipes and open channels conveyed water over short distances, such as the 0.7 km system at Knossos. In ancient Greece (6th century BC), advancements included long tunnels like the approximately 2.5 km Eupalinos Tunnel on Samos and inverted siphons at Pergamon, demonstrating early mastery of pressure management and subterranean routing. The Romans elevated aqueduct technology to unprecedented scales during the 1st century BC to 3rd century AD, constructing over 500 km of conduitsâincluding elevated arcades and siphonsâthat delivered approximately 1.13 million cubic meters of water per day to Rome alone via eleven major aqueducts, supporting a population of over one million with per capita supplies of 200â300 gallons daily. Notable Roman examples include the 16 km Aqua Appia (312 BC) and the 69 km Aqua Claudia, which featured towering bridges up to 28.5 meters high, as seen in the surviving Segovia Aqueduct in Spain. Byzantine and medieval engineers built upon these foundations, maintaining and extending Roman networks while introducing new systems, such as the approximately 268 km Valens Aqueduct system in Constantinople (completed 373 AD) and the 25 km Bottini tunnels in Siena, Italy, which relied on gravity-fed contour channels with regular maintenance shafts. In the modern era, aqueducts have adapted to larger scales and diverse terrains, incorporating pumps and reservoirs alongside gravity flow; the 444-mile California Aqueduct, operational since 1973, transports water from the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta to southern California to meet urban and agricultural demands in arid regions. Similarly, the 336-mile Central Arizona Project delivers Colorado River water across the desert, underscoring aqueducts' ongoing role in addressing water scarcity amid population growth and climate challenges. For detailed historical development, see the History section. Throughout history, these structures have not only sustained civilizations but also influenced urban planning, public health, and environmental management.
